effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive quantitative findings from the B.C. survey and qualitative findings from Ontario interviews; no inferential statistical tests or regression effect estimates are reported.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive quantitative and qualitative findings (no inferential causal/regression effect estimate reported): Among B.C. First Nations water operators answering certification adequacy (n = 76 of 79 surveyed), 44 (58%) were certified to the level required by their water system while 32 (42%) were uncertified or under-certified. Among 71 B.C. respondents answering job satisfaction, 53 reported being satisfied, 15 unsatisfied, and 3 both satisfied and unsatisfied; dissatisfaction was tied primarily to wages/hours (n = 6) and lack of funding/support (n = 6). Major reported operational challenges in B.C. were lack of support from band councils and lack of operation and maintenance (O&M) funding, alongside community complaints (n = 25), limited technical support (n = 19), difficulty obtaining supplies (n = 14), interpersonal conflicts with colleagues or band councils (n = 12), challenging plants (n = 10), and drinking water advisories (n = 8). Qualitatively in Ontario (n = 8 communities) and B.C., the 80:20 federal (AANDC)-to-community O&M cost-sharing structure, inadequate or non-ringfenced user fees ($80-$85/year for households and $500-$1,200/year for businesses in 3 of 7 full-scale Ontario systems), lack of budget transparency, political hiring/dismissal, and requirements for Chief and Council approval on routine purchases (including one refusal to allow chlorine purchase) impeded water system O&M and operator retention (at least 29 operators across 5 Ontario communities over 69 cumulative years).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 6-7, 10, Results; Tables 2-3 and Figure 5, PDF pp. 11-13; PDF pp. 14-16, Discussion

mechanism_certainty.comment: Mixed-methods study (design ceiling = 2) that directly documents administrative, budgetary, and local-federal governance mechanisms (80:20 AANDC/band O&M funding split, Chief and Council purchase-approval bottlenecks including blocked chlorine procurement, lack of regulatory wage standardization, and political hiring/dismissal) operating on First Nations drinking water treatment systems via primary operator interviews and surveys.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 6-7, 10, Results; PDF pp. 14-16, Discussion

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines intergovernmental O&M cost-sharing (80% AANDC / 20% local First Nation) and lack of regulatory standardization across jurisdictions (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination), Band Council discretionary control over budgets, purchase approvals, and hiring/dismissal (discretion, procedural_steps), household/business user fees for the 20% local O&M share (fees), and community complaints (complaint).

sample_size.comment: 8 operators interviewed across 8 southern Ontario First Nations communities (selected from 45 listed and 28 confirmed communities; employing 14 full-time and 4 part-time operators total) and 79 B.C. First Nations water treatment operators surveyed at an annual conference (with item-specific response counts such as n = 76 for certification adequacy, n = 72 for hours worked, n = 71 for job satisfaction, and n = 70 for years of experience).
sample_size.value: 87 water treatment plant operators (8 operators across 8 southern Ontario First Nations communities in semi-structured interviews; 79 British Columbia First Nations water treatment operators in structured questionnaires)

study_design.comment: Sequential mixed-methods design in which qualitative semi-structured interviews in Ontario informed a structured closed-answer questionnaire analyzed descriptively in British Columbia.
study_design.value: Sequential mixed-methods study combining qualitative semi-structured interviews (in Ontario) and cross-sectional structured surveys with descriptive quantitative analysis (in British Columbia)
